headline: Monhegan Mackerel Ball Up, Pollock Break Surface as Bass Start Sliding for the Rivers
subhead: The fall handoff is underway in Penobscot Bay — groundfish moving shallow, stripers staging at the river mouths, and the mackerel schools writing the whole story.
body_markdown:
Forty years working this water teaches you the same lesson every September: when the mackerel quit scattering thin and silvery and start balling up thick and dark on the surface, the season's turning whether the calendar agrees or not. Down at the co-op in Rockland this week the talk was exactly that — mackerel tightening up off Monhegan, pollock themselves busting bait on top of the ledges, and that combination has been as reliable a fall marker in this bay as any buoy reading for as long as anyone can remember.

The Gulf of Maine has been sliding toward its fall temperature pretty steadily, and we flagged that pattern last week — said it would keep accelerating over the next couple weeks as the water kept dropping, and that's exactly what's playing out now. Inshore surface temps are settling into the upper 50s in the coves and thoroughfares, with the open water off Monhegan and Matinicus still holding a touch warmer, low 60s in spots, which is why the mackerel and the pollock chasing them haven't pushed off the ledges yet. Wind's been mostly out of the northwest this week, which has kept the bay clean and the ledges fishable, but it's also the wind that starts pulling that warm surface layer apart and pushing bait toward the harbors. Watch for that shift.

Striped bass are doing what they do this time of year — sliding off the open ledges and tightening up around river mouths and estuary mouths as peanut bunker and juvenile herring start their exit. The Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, and the upper reaches around Boothbay Harbor itself have all been holding fish on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, when bait gets flushed out past the pinch points. Nothing blitz-sized, but a mate working out of Boothbay described steady action on schoolie-to-mid-20-inch bass on 3-inch white or chartreuse soft plastics fished on light jig heads, worked slow along the current seams where the river water meets the salt. A few better fish, mid-30s, have come on live mackerel drifted near the ledges off Damariscove Island on the last of the ebb, fished on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in 20 to 30 feet.

The groundfish story is the one worth paying closest attention to right now. Pollock have been showing thick on the surface around Monhegan's ledges — the Washerwoman and White Head both producing — chasing mackerel and sand eels up into the top 20 feet of water on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current rips hardest off the point. Diamond jigs, the standard 4- to 6-ounce chrome and green, worked with a fast vertical retrieve right through the surface commotion, have been taking pollock to 8 pounds without much trouble when the birds are working. Cod have been harder to come by close to shore, but the deeper channels through Penobscot Bay — the water off Vinalhaven toward the Fox Island Thorofare, and the deeper stretches between Isle au Haut and Stonington — are still holding fish in the 80- to 120-foot range. That's bottom-fishing water: clam bait or cut mackerel on a standard cod rig, fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide when the current isn't ripping you off the structure. Haddock have been mixed in with those cod on the same drifts, mostly undersized but enough keepers coming up to make it worth the run out of Stonington or Deer Isle.

Bluefish have been the wildcard. There's been a scattered push of them working the mouths of the bigger rivers and around the outer islands, likely riding the same bait movement pushing the bass around, but nobody's calling it consistent yet — more a fish here, a fish there, mixed in with the striper bite rather than its own dedicated pattern. Worth a few casts with a metal lure if you're already working the river mouths on bass, but don't plan a trip around it.

Eastern Egg Rock's bass and bluefish action has been steady rather than spectacular this week, which tracks with everything else happening in the bay — fish are transitioning, not committing hard yet. The puffins have mostly cleared out for the season, but the rock still holds bait and bass will sit on the structure around it on a strong tide, particularly the top of the flood when water's pushing bait up against the ledges from the south side.

Looking at the next several days, the wind pattern holding out of the northwest should keep conditions workable through the weekend, with tides building toward the upcoming moon adding some push to both the bay currents and the river outflows. That's good news for the striper pattern at the river mouths — more current means more bait getting flushed, which means a better window for those last two hours of the ebb. Offshore, if the ledges around Monhegan keep holding pollock on the surface the way they have this week, that bite should only strengthen as more mackerel push south and get squeezed against the island. The bigger question is how fast the surface layer cools once this northwest wind really digs in — once it does, expect the bass to commit harder to the rivers and the groundfish to push a little deeper. For now, the smart move is working the ebb at the river mouths for bass and hitting Monhegan on a calm morning for pollock and mackerel while the window's still open.
